title: This Butterfly Lives Almost a Year—and Barely Ages!
summary: Did you know most butterflies live just a few weeks? But one group from Central and South America breaks all the rules. Meet the Heliconius butterflies—they can live almost a whole year! One kind, called Heliconius hewitsoni, lived 348 days. That's 25 times longer than its close cousin, which only made it 14 days. Scientists from the University of Bristol wanted to know why. They tested the butterflies' grip strength—like a handshake test for bugs. Older Heliconius hecale butterflies were just as strong as young ones. They barely seemed to age! Another species, Dryas iulia, got weaker as it got older. So what's the secret? Heliconius butterflies eat pollen, not just nectar. Pollen gives them extra protein. But here's the twist: even when scientists took pollen away, these butterflies still lived longer. So it's not just diet—their bodies evolved to age slowly. This is a big deal for science. By studying these butterflies, researchers hope to learn how to help people stay healthier as they get older. Imagine if we could unlock the secret to slow aging! What would you do with an extra-long, healthy life?
why_it_matters: If scientists learn how these butterflies delay aging, they might find ways to keep your grandparents playful and full of energy for many more family adventures.

background_read: Scientists have long studied aging in animals like mice and flies to understand why our bodies wear out. Researchers at the University of Bristol (a university in England) turned to Heliconius butterflies, which are known for their long lifespans. These butterflies live in tropical forests from Mexico to Argentina, where they feed on pollen that provides extra protein, possibly helping them stay youthful.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from the University of Bristol, and Heliconius butterflies.
WHAT: Heliconius butterflies can live up to 348 days and maintain grip strength while barely aging.
WHERE: Forests of Central and South America, and a lab in England.
WHY: Studying their slow aging could unlock ways to help people stay healthier as they grow older.

perspectives.description: Unlocking the secrets of butterflies' slow aging could lead to breakthroughs in medicine, helping humans live healthier into old age.
Butterfly biology differs greatly from humans, so what works for them might not translate to people.
Studying a wide range of animals lets scientists compare how aging evolved, building a bigger picture of life itself.
